I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so I will keep to the cropping pattern I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize. At my age, I want something steady, familiar, and not too risky. This rotation fits my land, the local weather, and the irrigation conditions I am used to managing. Wheat gives me a secure winter crop, and maize follows well after harvest. I do not want to spread myself across too many crops because that increases labor, timing pressure, and market uncertainty.

For wheat, I will keep improved seed rather than old saved seed because I want better stand uniformity and more stable yield. I will do rotary tillage before sowing, put most of the phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, and split nitrogen so the crop has enough early growth but does not become too lush before spring. I will irrigate around key stages: after sowing if moisture is short, at jointing, and at grain filling if needed. I will spray only as needed, mainly for weeds early and for disease or aphids if pressure appears.

After wheat harvest, I will plant summer maize quickly to catch heat and moisture. I will use hybrid maize because I care most about yield and uniform ears. I will keep field operations simple, again using rotary tillage so I can turn the field around fast after wheat. Fertilizer will be moderate but solid, with nitrogen carrying most of the yield, and I will irrigate mainly around establishment and the big demand period before and around tasseling if rainfall is not enough. Pest control will stay limited to a few necessary applications because I do not want unnecessary cost. This is the plan I would follow because it matches my experience, my labor capacity, and the conditions of my area.
